opus-5.5.text:
Well, honestly, it came from a realization that this was too big a space for one group to explore alone. When we started looking at neural network weights as a data modality in their own right, treating trained models as objects you can learn from, we quickly saw that the interesting questions weren't going to be answered by a single paper or a single lab. You need lots of trained models, diverse architectures, different training conditions, and that's expensive to produce and hard to standardize.

So one of the first things we did was think about the community side. We built model zoos, large, structured collections of trained networks with recorded training trajectories and hyperparameters, and we wanted other people to use them. If everybody generates their own little population of models with their own quirks, you can't compare results, and the field doesn't really form. A shared dataset gives people a common ground. That's what happened in computer vision with ImageNet, and we felt weight-space learning needed something similar.

There's also a more personal reason. When you're early in a new direction, you're not even sure you're asking the right questions. Bringing in people from other areas, like people working on generative models, on representation learning, on theory around symmetries in weight space, challenges your assumptions very quickly. Someone looks at what you're doing and says, "Why aren't you accounting for permutation symmetries?" or "Couldn't you generate weights instead of just analyzing them?" And those conversations pushed the work much further than we would have gotten on our own.

And frankly, I think it's just more fun. Organizing workshops, sharing data, co-authoring with people who see the problem differently, that energy is what turns an idea into a research area rather than a niche curiosity.

r001.rationale: The response says that early in a new direction, he was unsure whether they were asking the right questions, and that input from other researchers quickly challenged their assumptions. This communicates involving others to check whether the idea was meaningful.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it came out of a kind of healthy skepticism about ourselves, honestly. When we started looking at neural network weights as a data modality in their own right, as something you could actually learn from rather than just the byproduct of training, the first reaction we got from a lot of people was, "Why would you do that? The weights are just the weights." And I think that's exactly the moment where you need other people in the room.

So part of it was the standard scientific reason: we wanted to make sure what we were seeing was real. When you train thousands of small networks and you start seeing structure in the weight space, structure that lets you predict things like test accuracy or the hyperparameters that were used, there's always the worry that you've just picked up on an artifact of your own setup. Having colleagues with different backgrounds, different training pipelines, different intuitions, poke at it early was a way of stress-testing the idea before we invested years in it.

The second reason was more practical. This kind of work is incredibly compute- and data-hungry in an unusual way. You don't need one big model, you need populations of models, and you need them to be diverse. No single group is going to generate all of that in a meaningful way. So building what we ended up calling model zoos was something that only made sense as a collaborative effort from day one. If we had done it alone, the data would have been too narrow and the conclusions would have been too narrow.

And the third reason, which I think is maybe the most important one, is that the questions you can ask about weight space cut across subfields. You've got people from optimization who care about loss landscapes, people from representation learning who want to encode the weights, people from the generative side who want to sample new models, people from security who think about backdoors in weights. None of us had all of that expertise. Bringing those people in early meant the research questions got shaped by that diversity, rather than us coming up with a framework in isolation and then trying to sell it afterwards.

So in short: we involved others early because we didn't trust ourselves enough to be right alone, and because the problem itself was too big and too interdisciplinary to be anything other than a community effort.

r001.rationale: Borth says they involved colleagues early to stress-test the idea and make sure the patterns they saw in neural network weights were real, directly explaining that they wanted to check whether the work was meaningful.

We were asking what we could learn by looking directly at the weights of a neural network, and that brings together questions about representation, optimization, and how you compare different networks. I wanted to involve other researchers early so we could challenge our assumptions and explore those questions together. When you’re working in a space like that, having different perspectives helps you figure out which observations are meaningful and which might just be artifacts of your experiments.

sol-6.1.text: Because we were entering a space where there were far more questions than answers. We wanted to understand what the weights of a trained neural network could tell us, and we felt it was important to bring in different perspectives early. If you work on that in isolation, it’s easy to get attached to your own interpretation. Involving other researchers helped us challenge our assumptions and explore which questions were actually worth pursuing.
